en.note:
The idea

Modal verbs are the Dutch equivalents of can, may, must, want to and shall/will: they're used together with another verb in the infinitive. The key rule is about position, and it's where Dutch is very different from English: the conjugated modal is in second place, and the infinitive goes to the end of the sentence. The two parts form a kind of "frame" around everything else.

Ik wil morgen met de trein naar Gent gaan. (I want to go to Ghent by train tomorrow.)

What each one means

  • kunnen: can, to be able to, to be possible. Ik kan zwemmen (I can swim). Kun je morgen komen? (Can you come tomorrow?)
  • mogen: may, to be allowed to. Mag ik hier parkeren? (May I park here?). niet mogen = not allowed: Je mag hier niet roken (you can't smoke here).
  • moeten: must, to have to. Ik moet werken. Careful: "I don't have to" is a different verb, hoeven, which you'll see later.
  • willen: to want. Ik wil koffie. To ask politely, add graag: Ik wil graag koffie (I'd like a coffee).
  • zullen: future, a promise or an offer. Ik zal je helpen (I'll help you). Zal ik je helpen? (Shall I help you?)

Conjugation

Modals are irregular in the singular: with ik, hij and zij they have no -t.

kunnenmoetenwillenmogenzullen
ikkanmoetwilmagzal
jij / ukunt / kanmoetwilt / wilmagzult / zal
hij / zijkanmoetwilmagzal
wij / jullie / zijkunnenmoetenwillenmogenzullen

Without the infinitive

With movement the infinitive is often left out, because it's obvious: Ik moet naar huis (I have to go home), Ik wil naar Brugge (I want to go to Bruges).

Watch out: typical mistakes for English speakers

  • Putting the infinitive right after the modal, as in English: Ik wil gaan morgen naar Gent → Ik wil morgen naar Gent gaan.
  • False friend: ik wil means "I want", not "I will". "I will" is ik zal.
  • Adding -t with hij: hij kant → hij kan.
  • Using "te" as in "to go": Ik wil te gaan → Ik wil gaan. No te after a modal.
en.vlaams: For the future, spoken Dutch uses gaan + infinitive a lot, just like English "going to": "Ik ga dat morgen doen" (I'm going to do that tomorrow). "Ge moogt" (= je mag, you may) is typically Flemish.
